interpretations.rationale: The source account is that a leader takes on a duty when it postpones a received ReadIndex request: pendingReadIndexMessages holds requests that cannot yet be answered because no entry of the leader's term is committed, and they are released when the term's first commit is observed (raft.go:1550-1554 calls releasePendingReadIndexMessages immediately before bcastAppend under the comment 'committed index has progressed for the term, so it is safe to respond to pending read index requests'). The same enabling change of state - raftLog.committed advancing to an entry of the leader's term - is also produced inside switchToConfig, which calls r.maybeCommit() and, on success, only calls bcastAppend (raft.go:2013-2028). Applying a committed configuration change is a legal producer of that path: applyConfChange -> switchToConfig is invoked by the application whenever a configuration change is observed in Ready.CommittedEntries. When the applied change makes ProgressTracker.Committed() exceed raftLog.committed (removing a voter that is unreachable, or leaving a joint configuration whose outgoing half contains such a voter) and the entry at the resulting index carries the leader's term, the commit is performed with the postponed request still unreleased. Because the request was stored in pendingReadIndexMessages and not in readOnly.unconfirmedReads, no later heartbeat can carry its context, so the duty is not discharged by the periodic heartbeat round: the received request yields no ReadState for a local read and no MsgReadIndexResp for a forwarded one until an unrelated entry is committed (which again goes through the MsgAppResp path) or the client retries. The defect is therefore a lost duty on one of two enabling paths, scoped to a bounded interval: from the postponed request until the next commit outside switchToConfig. The returned index remains safe whenever the request is eventually released, because the recorded index is taken from raftLog.committed at release time and raftLog.committed never decreases; the defect is a bounded-liveness (unanswered request) issue, not a stale-read safety violation. A native draft probe of both variants (removing an unreachable voter, and leaving a joint configuration) reproduced the observable sequence: the leader postponed the request (pending_reads=1, committed_entry_term 1, leader term 2), then applying the committed change advanced committed 10 -> 11 with committed_entry_term 2 == leader term while pending_reads stayed 1, no ReadState was produced, the delayed acknowledgement of the previous configuration (match_3=11) did not release it, a heartbeat round carried no read context (heartbeat_ctx_len 0) and did not release it, and only an unrelated proposal committed by the new configuration released the request (read_states 1, request ctx A, index 12 - the later commit index, i.e. answered late rather than answered wrong). interpretations.rationale: The source account: tracker.IsSingleton (tracker/tracker.go:158-162) is a size test - one member in Voters[0] and none in Voters[1] - and its doc comment asserts that this member is the leader, but nothing compares it with the local node id. stepLeader's MsgReadIndex case (raft.go:1354-1361) takes that test as sufficient authority to answer immediately from r.raftLog.committed, for a local request by appending a ReadState and for a forwarded request by sending MsgReadIndexResp, without any heartbeat or readOnly round. The library reaches this state legitimately: applying a committed configuration change that removes the local node while it is leading leaves it leading unless Config.StepDownOnRemoval is set (raft.go:1985-2012 with the documented default false at raft.go:282-287), and its tracker then holds a configuration whose only voter is another node. The same library refuses new proposals from exactly this node (raft.go:1294-1303: 'If we are not currently a member of the range (i.e. this node was removed from the configuration while serving as leader), drop any new proposals'), so the responsibility for the removed leader's behaviour is taken up on the write path and left open on the read path. The consequence is a safety claim, not a progress claim: ReadOnlySafe is documented as achieving linearizability by communicating with the quorum (raft.go:233-244) and ReadIndex promises that work issued before the request can be served once the application has advanced past the returned index (node.go:218-224, README.md:27-32). A client that issues its read through the removed leader - a node that still reports itself as the leader - is handed an index that is below entries already committed by the actual leader of that configuration, so the state it is licensed to serve may miss a write that completed before the read began, and retrying at the same node reproduces the same answer instead of repairing it. The draft probe exercises both halves: it observes the removed leader (config voters=(2), singleton true, is_voter false, still StateLeader) answering MsgReadIndex with read index 2 while the actual leader had already committed index 4, emitting no message at all, and it observes the same request answered by the actual leader with an index that covers its commit index; three later heartbeat intervals produce no reply and the removed leader repeats the same stale index. The formal execution of this harness is requested with this update, so this remains a source-grounded account until its receipt exists.
counterevidence: A client is expected to direct linearizable reads at the current leader; reading through a node that was removed is a client-side premise. The library cannot detect staleness in general: a leader that was removed by a configuration change it has already applied, or one partitioned away, also answers old-term requests until it hears a higher term.

What makes this case the library's responsibility rather than the client's is narrower: the shortcut is taken from the local tracker, which already establishes that the only voter is another node, and the library refuses proposals from that same node; without the shortcut the read would need a quorum acknowledgement from the current configuration, and the removed leader cannot obtain one once the actual leader has moved to a higher term (its heartbeat is ignored or answered with a higher term).
limitations: The scenario requires the application to apply a committed configuration change that removes the leading node while Config.StepDownOnRemoval is false; applications that set that option, or that stop the removed node, do not reach it.

The removed leader remains at its old term only while nothing from the current configuration carries a higher term to it; with CheckQuorum or PreVote enabled the current leader answers the stale heartbeat with its higher term and the removed leader steps down, which bounds the window but does not remove the stale answers issued before that.
